title: Delhi High Court: FSSAI Cannot Regulate Cattle Feed, Quashes Mandatory BIS Certification
meta_description: Delhi High Court holds FSSAI's mandate covers human food only, striking down its cattle feed regulation and the BIS certification it had made mandatory.
case_name: Godrej Agrovet Ltd. v. Food Safety and Standards Authority of India & Anr.
citation: W.P.(C) 1079/2025, neutral citation 2026:DHC:2861-DB, judgment dated 7 April 2026
body: A ruling with direct consequences for animal feed manufacturers and dairy businesses has settled a question that had sat unresolved for years: whether the Food Safety and Standards Authority of India can regulate what goes into cattle and poultry feed at all. The Delhi High Court answered no, in a judgment delivered on 7 April 2026 in Godrej Agrovet Ltd. v. Food Safety and Standards Authority of India & Anr.

That dispute arose from a set of FSSAI directives issued between December 2019 and January 2021 that restricted the use of meat and bone meal in feed given to milk and meat producing animals, and from a note to Regulation 2.5.2 that effectively made Bureau of Indian Standards certification mandatory for animal feed products. Godrej Agrovet, a major animal feed manufacturer, challenged both the restriction and the certification mandate as beyond FSSAI's statutory authority under the Food Safety and Standards Act, 2006. Feed manufacturers had complied with these circulars for years on the footing that FSSAI's jurisdiction over animal feed was settled, a footing Godrej Agrovet's petition asked the court to test directly against the statute's own definition of food rather than assume.

The court's reasoning turned on the Act's own definition of food. Reading the statute as a whole, the bench held that the FSS Act was drafted to regulate food meant for human consumption, and that animal feed does not fall within that definition merely because the animals in question eventually enter the human food chain as dairy or meat. On that basis, the court found that FSSAI had exceeded its jurisdiction when it issued binding directives governing the composition of cattle feed, and it quashed the restrictions on meat and bone meal along with the underlying note to Regulation 2.5.2.

On the BIS certification point, the court drew a separate but related line. It held that making any Bureau of Indian Standards specification mandatory is a function the law assigns to the Central Government, not to the Food Authority acting on its own. Without a specific central government direction making a BIS standard compulsory, FSSAI could not convert what Parliament left as a voluntary standard into a mandatory compliance burden for feed manufacturers through its own directive. The certification mandate was quashed on this ground as well.

The judgment, delivered by a bench led by Chief Justice Devendra Kumar Upadhyaya along with Justice Tejas Karia, did not leave animal feed entirely outside regulatory reach. It recognised that feed safety could still be addressed through a properly framed mechanism, whether under a different statute or through rules that the Central Government itself chooses to make binding, rather than through FSSAI directives issued without that backing.

For feed manufacturers, the immediate effect is that compliance built around the quashed directives and the BIS mandate no longer has a legal basis, at least until a replacement framework is notified through the correct statutory route. Businesses that had absorbed the cost of mandatory BIS certification, or restructured their formulations to avoid using meat and bone meal under the quashed directives, can now reassess those decisions against what current law actually requires rather than what the quashed directives demanded.

The ruling also carries a wider lesson for regulatory practice beyond this one sector. A food or feed business facing an FSSAI directive that appears to stretch past what the parent Act defines as its subject matter now has a concrete precedent for arguing that the directive is ultra vires, rather than treating every FSSAI circular as automatically binding regardless of its statutory footing.

FSSAI retains full authority over products meant for human consumption, including dairy and meat products derived from animals that may have been fed under the now quashed regime. What the judgment removes is FSSAI's claimed power to reach back into animal feed itself as though it were human food, a distinction the court treated as fundamental to how far the statute actually extends.
why_it_matters: The ruling draws a firm boundary around FSSAI's jurisdiction, confirming it cannot regulate animal feed as though it were human food and cannot make BIS certification mandatory without a specific Central Government direction. Animal feed manufacturers who built compliance programmes around the quashed directives should review whether those measures remain legally required, and food businesses more broadly now have a clearer basis to challenge FSSAI directives that exceed what the FSS Act's definitions actually cover.
card_summary: Delhi High Court quashed FSSAI's restrictions on meat and bone meal in cattle feed and its mandatory BIS certification mandate, holding the FSS Act's food definition covers human consumption only.
card_tip: If an FSSAI directive affects a product not meant for human consumption, check whether it falls within the FSS Act's definition of food before treating it as binding.
verification_notes: Selected for the Food Safety & FSSAI practice area because this ruling settles a long-pending jurisdictional question for the animal feed industry and is not yet covered on the site, which has FSSAI guides on human food licensing and enforcement but nothing on the FSS Act's reach over animal feed. No specific Delhi NCR or Kolkata angle was found and none is forced; the ruling applies nationally to feed manufacturers. Case name, citation (2026:DHC:2861-DB), W.P.(C) 1079/2025, the 7 April 2026 date, and the core holdings (FSS Act limited to human food, BIS mandate requires Central Government notification) are confirmed across three independent reports (Bar and Bench, Verdictum, ThePrint). The bench composition (Chief Justice Devendra Kumar Upadhyaya and Justice Tejas Karia) is reported by Verdictum and corroborated by a second outlet (medicaldialogues.in); this is treated as adequately confirmed for the body but the full 45-page judgment text was not independently opened, so niche procedural details beyond the reported holdings are not stated.
